name: Leuprolide
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in several brands and depot strengths for advanced prostate cancer, endometriosis, fibroid-related anemia and central precocious puberty, each backed by its own clinical studies.
summary: Leuprolide is a synthetic GnRH agonist that shuts down sex hormone production. It treats prostate cancer, endometriosis and early puberty.
keyTakeaway: Leuprolide is a lab-made version of GnRH, the brain hormone that switches on the testes and ovaries. Given continuously, it does the opposite of the natural pulses: after a brief surge, the pituitary stops responding and testosterone or estrogen falls to very low levels. It is FDA-approved under brands such as Lupron Depot and Eligard for advanced prostate cancer, endometriosis, fibroid-related anemia and early puberty in children. In a pediatric trial, a 3-month injection suppressed the puberty hormone LH in 78 to 95% of children. Hot flashes, the initial flare, and bone loss with longer use are the main trade-offs.

blocks.text: Leuprolide (called leuprorelin outside the United States) is a synthetic peptide modeled on gonadotropin-releasing hormone, or GnRH. GnRH is made in the hypothalamus, a small region at the base of the brain, and tells the pituitary gland to release the two hormones that drive the testes and ovaries: luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) [2].

Most leuprolide is given as a depot, a slow-release injection that keeps working for weeks or months. AbbVie's Lupron Depot comes in strengths that last 1, 3, 4 or 6 months for prostate cancer [2]. Tolmar sells Eligard, injected under the skin, for the same cancer [6], and separate pediatric products exist for early puberty [4].

Leuprolide grew out of a race to decode the brain's control of the pituitary. Andrew Schally and Roger Guillemin, working in rival laboratories, each isolated the hypothalamic releasing hormone for LH in 1971, an effort that took hundreds of thousands of pig brains. The work earned them a share of the 1977 Nobel Prize [1].

The same year the hormone was isolated, Schally's group showed that it could also suppress gonadotropin release, and experiments in monkeys showed that a constant supply of the hormone desensitized its receptors on the pituitary. That paradox, a stimulating hormone used to switch the system off, opened the way to synthetic analogs. Schally ran the first clinical studies in Mexico in 1972, and the first study of an agonist in prostate cancer was published in 1982 [1].

The body releases natural GnRH in short pulses. Leuprolide binds the same receptor on the pituitary but stays active far longer. In the first days, this triggers a surge of LH and FSH, and testosterone in men can climb about 50% above baseline [2]. With continuous exposure, the pituitary stops responding, LH and FSH fall, and the testes or ovaries largely stop making sex hormones. The label notes the effect reverses once the drug is stopped [2].

That shutdown is the point. Prostate cancer growth is fueled by testosterone, endometriosis tissue by estrogen, and early puberty by hormones switching on too soon. In the main prostate cancer study of the 1-month depot, testosterone dropped into the castrate range (50 ng/dL or lower) within 30 days in 94% of men [2].

Yes. Leuprolide is FDA-approved in several brands and strengths, each with its own label. Lupron Depot at 7.5, 22.5, 30 and 45 mg treats advanced prostate cancer [2]. The 3.75 mg monthly Lupron Depot treats endometriosis and, with iron, anemia caused by uterine fibroids before surgery [3]. Lupron Depot-PED treats central precocious puberty [4], and Eligard is approved for advanced prostate cancer [6]. Generic leuprolide acetate is also available.

items: Advanced prostate cancer, to lower testosterone that drives tumor growth [2]
Endometriosis, to relieve pain and shrink lesions, often paired with norethindrone acetate to limit bone loss [3]
Anemia from uterine fibroids, together with iron, to improve blood counts before surgery [3]
Central precocious puberty, when puberty starts unusually early because the brain's signal switches on too soon [4]

blocks.text: In children with precocious puberty, a phase 3 trial gave a 3-month depot of 11.25 mg or 30 mg to 84 children. The puberty hormone LH stayed suppressed from months 2 to 6 in 78.4% of the lower-dose group and 95.2% of the higher-dose group, and growth rates and side effects were similar between doses [5].
For endometriosis, the label limits total treatment with the 3.75 mg depot plus add-back hormone therapy to 12 months because of concerns about bone density [3].

Most side effects follow from low sex hormones. In men with prostate cancer, common reactions reported in more than 10% included hot flashes and sweats, general pain, injection site reactions, digestive complaints, swelling and urinary symptoms [2]. In women treated for endometriosis, hot flashes, headache, vaginal inflammation, mood changes, weight change, nausea, lower libido and dizziness were each reported by more than 10% [3].

The early testosterone surge can briefly worsen prostate cancer symptoms, including bone pain and, rarely, spinal cord compression [2]. Labels also warn of metabolic changes such as raised blood sugar and lipids, a reported increase in heart attack and stroke risk in men, effects on heart rhythm, seizures, and severe skin reactions [2]. In women, bone mineral density loss limits how long it can be used, and it can harm a pregnancy [3]. Children may have emotional swings and, early on, a flare of puberty signs [4].
